newsitem.title: USA: Commodities plummet as rate, supply worries fade.
newsitem.headline: Commodities plummet as rate, supply worries fade.

text.p: Oil, grain and metal prices fell sharply on Thursday as prospects for adequate supplies and rallies in stocks and bonds on less concern about interest rates prompted speculators to exit commodity investments.

"With the bond market strong on evidence the U.S. economy is slowing, and inflation no threat, there's little incentive for investors in precious metals or commodities in general right now," Smith Barney analyst Phil Tiger said.
U.S. economic news Thursday did nothing to signal higher interest rates, with jobless claims in the week ended October 26 higher-than-expected at 342,000. U.S. bond yields fell.
On Wednesday the fall in U.S. third quarter economic growth to an annual 2.2 pct pace had already suggested the economy was slowing with little threat of inflation seen.
Oil prices meanwhile led a rout in energy markets, with crude falling nearly a dollar a barrel as the possibility that an Iraqi deal with the United Nations to sell oil may revive.
Corn and soybean prices also fell sharply on ideas that this fall's harvest would come in bigger than expected.
Gold and silver prices also fell as investors worried little about inflation lacked any incentive to hedge their bets with buying "hard" assets.

The result was widespread selling by speculative funds that drove the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures down 3.83 points to close at 237.83, down 1.6 percent and at its lowest since October 1995.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices went into a steep decline and broke the back of a four-and-a-half month rally that had taken crude oil to six year highs.
December crude oil closed 93 cents a barrel lower at $23.35, with November heating oil ending down 2.12 cents a gallon at 66.34 cents and November unleaded gasoline down 3.44 cents at 66.56 cents.
"This is meltdown," said broker Tim Holmes at MeesPierson Derivatives. "It's more than your average correction."

Sparking the freefall was news that rival Kurdish factions agreed to extend a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that ended two months of clashes in northern Iraq, which in turn revived talk that a United Nations deal to allow Iraq to sell a limited amount of oil to obtain food would go forward.
That deal was frozen after Iraqi troops aided a faction of Kurdish fighters in August.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices also fell sharply as clear weather improved harvest prospects and optimism about this year's corn and soybean crops grew.
"The market is more concerned about the potential for a bigger crop than it is with demand right now," said Mark Cermak of Chicago trading house O'Connor and Co.

On Thursday the Agriculture Department reported higher-than-expected weekly exports for the week ended October 24 of 810,100 tonnes. But exporters were still selling futures, which traders took as a bearish sign.
December corn fell 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $2.66.

Wheat prices also fell, with traders nervous about a report that a crop-spoiling fungus, karnal bunt, was detected in Tennessee wheat. December wheat closed 9-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.71-1/4 cents on fears this would hit exports.
Metals also closed lower on speculative selling, with economic news providing no incentives for metals investors.

December silver at the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division closed down 2.0 cents at $4.808 an ounce after an early low at $4.760, the lowest level for the December contract in two years. December gold ended down $2.20 at $379.10 after setting a life-of-contract low at $377.70.
"The silver market appears weak at the moment and could give way to longer term support at $4.72," CPM Group analyst Edward Kemp said.
